steps.body: Given three addends, decide for yourself which two to join first — and be able to say why that pair was the best choice.
steps.narration: Given three addends, decide for yourself which two to join first — and be able to say why that pair was the best choice.

widget.prompt: You chose 8 and 2 as your pair. Fill the frame to check they make ten.
widget.missFeedback: Fill one square at a time, counting as you go.

widget.prompt: To add 7 + 3 + 5, which two should you group first?

options.label: 7 and 3
options.feedback: Correct — 7 and 3 make exactly ten, which leaves an easy ten-plus-5 to finish.

options.label: 7 and 5
options.feedback: This pair does not land on ten, so the last step stays awkward.

options.label: 3 and 5
options.feedback: This pair misses the ten that 7 and 3 would have made together.

options.label: No pair helps here
options.feedback: One pair does make ten; scanning for ten-partners first is the whole strategy.

hints: Look for two addends that make ten.
Ten plus the rest is easy to name.

widget.prompt: In 8 + 2 + 4, why is grouping 8 and 2 first a smart choice?

options.label: It leaves an easy ten-plus-4 step
options.feedback: Correct — 8 and 2 make exactly ten, which leaves an easy ten-plus-4 to finish.

options.label: It skips 2 and pairs 8 with 4 instead
options.feedback: 8 and 4 make 12, not ten, so the last step stays awkward — 8 and 2 is the pair that lands on ten.

options.label: It lets you ignore the 4 completely
options.feedback: The 4 still has to join the total; grouping 8 and 2 first just makes that last step easy, not optional.

options.label: It makes every group of three addends equal ten
options.feedback: Only this particular pair happens to make ten; scanning for ten-partners first is the whole strategy, not a guarantee for every problem.
